3. EXPLORATORY DATA ANALYSIS¶

3. Exploratory Data Analysis — Overview

Structure:

  • 3.1 target distribution
  • 3.2 key numerical vars (Amt, DT)
  • 3.3 categoricals (tiered by cardinality)
  • 3.4 missingness map (C/D/M/V/Other)
  • 3.5 missingness as signal
  • 3.6 V-column correlation/redundancy
  • 3.7 Numerical Variables (C, D) — Distribution and Outliers

Throughout: findings are backed by sample size and, where relevant, statistical significance — not visual impression alone.

3.1 Target variable — distribution and class imbalance¶

Starting point for everything that follows: how imbalanced is the target, and what does that imply for metric choice and modeling strategy going forward.

In [8]:
# 3.1 Target variable — distribution and class imbalance

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))

counts = df_train['isFraud'].value_counts()
labels = ['Legitimate', 'Fraud']
percentages = counts / len(df_train)

# Bar chart
ax.bar(labels, counts.values,
       color=[COLORS['legit'], COLORS['fraud']], width=0.5)
ax.set_title('Transaction Count by Class')
ax.set_ylabel('Number of transactions')

# Add counts + percentages on top of bars
for i, (v, p) in enumerate(zip(counts.values, percentages.values)):
    ax.text(i, v + 5000,
            f'{v:,}\n({p:.2%})',
            ha='center', fontweight='bold', fontsize=10)

plt.suptitle('Target Variable (isFraud) — Severe Class Imbalance',
             fontweight='bold', fontsize=13)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Legitimate transactions : {counts[0]:,}  ({percentages[0]:.2%})")
print(f"Fraudulent transactions : {counts[1]:,}  ({percentages[1]:.2%})")
print(f"\nImbalance ratio        : {counts[0]/counts[1]:.0f}:1")

Legitimate transactions : 569,877  (96.50%)
Fraudulent transactions : 20,663  (3.50%)

Imbalance ratio        : 28:1

3.1 Closing note

96.5%/3.5% split, ~28:1 imbalance — accuracy is meaningless here (a dummy classifier already scores 96.5%). This is why AUC-ROC and cost-based metrics drive model selection throughout Section 6, and why the cost-benefit framework in Section 7 — not a default 0.5 threshold — determines the operating point.

3.2 Key Numerical Variables — TransactionAmt¶

3.2.1 Key Numerical Variables — TransactionAmt¶

First numerical variable examined: transaction amount. Checking whether fraud clusters in a particular price range, and whether fraud/legit transactions differ in typical size.

In [9]:
# 3.2 Key Numerical Variables — TransactionAmt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(12, 12))

bins = [0, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, df_train['TransactionAmt'].max() + 1]
labels = [f'${bins[i]}–${bins[i+1]}' for i in range(len(bins)-2)] + [f'${bins[-2]:.0f}+']

fraud = df_train[df_train['isFraud'] == 1]['TransactionAmt']
legit = df_train[df_train['isFraud'] == 0]['TransactionAmt']

fraud_counts, _ = np.histogram(fraud, bins=bins)
legit_counts, _ = np.histogram(legit, bins=bins)
counts = fraud_counts + legit_counts


total_fraud = len(fraud)

# Plot 1: COUNT of transactions 
x = range(len(counts))
axes[0].bar(x, legit_counts,
            color=COLORS['legit'], alpha=0.7,
            edgecolor='black', linewidth=1.2, width=0.6)
axes[0].bar(x, fraud_counts,
            bottom=legit_counts,
            color=COLORS['fraud'], alpha=0.9,
            edgecolor='black', linewidth=1.2, width=0.6)
axes[0].set_title('TransactionAmt Distribution — Counts',
                  fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Transaction Amount Range ($)', fontsize=11)
axes[0].set_ylabel('Count', fontsize=11)
axes[0].set_xticks(x)
axes[0].set_xticklabels(labels, rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=10)

for i in range(len(counts)):
    axes[0].text(i, legit_counts[i] / 2,
                 f'{legit_counts[i]:,}',
                 ha='center', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    if fraud_counts[i] > 0:
        axes[0].text(i,
                     legit_counts[i] + fraud_counts[i] + counts.max() * 0.02,
                     f'{fraud_counts[i]:,}',
                     ha='center', fontsize=10,
                     color=COLORS['fraud'], fontweight='bold')

# Plot 2: % of fraud (relative to all fraud)
fraud_pct_of_fraud = fraud_counts / total_fraud * 100
axes[1].bar(x, fraud_pct_of_fraud,
            color=COLORS['fraud'], alpha=0.9,
            edgecolor='black', linewidth=1.2, width=0.6)
axes[1].set_title('Fraud Distribution — % of All Fraud Transactions',
                  fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Transaction Amount Range ($)', fontsize=11)
axes[1].set_ylabel('% of Fraud Transactions', fontsize=11)
axes[1].set_xticks(x)
axes[1].set_xticklabels(labels, rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=10)

for i, fp in enumerate(fraud_pct_of_fraud):
    axes[1].text(i, fp + 0.5, f'{fp:.2f}%',
                 ha='center', fontsize=10,
                 fontweight='bold', color=COLORS['fraud'])

# Plot 3: Fraud vs Legit — mean amount comparison
mean_amt = df_train.groupby('isFraud')['TransactionAmt'].mean()
axes[2].bar(['Legitimate', 'Fraud'], mean_amt.values,
            color=[COLORS['legit'], COLORS['fraud']], width=0.5)
axes[2].set_title('Average Transaction Amount by Class',
                  fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
axes[2].set_ylabel('Mean TransactionAmt ($)', fontsize=11)

for i, v in enumerate(mean_amt.values):
    axes[2].text(i, v + (v * 0.03), f'${v:,.2f}',
                 ha='center', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Sanity check: confirm the histogram captures every transaction
assert fraud_counts.sum() == total_fraud, "Fraud histogram is dropping transactions"
assert legit_counts.sum() == len(legit), "Legit histogram is dropping transactions"
print(f"Max TransactionAmt: ${df_train['TransactionAmt'].max():,.2f}")
print(f"All {total_fraud:,} fraud and {len(legit):,} legit transactions accounted for.")

Max TransactionAmt: $31,937.39
All 20,663 fraud and 569,877 legit transactions accounted for.

Fraud concentrates in the USD 20-200 range (67% of all fraud cases fall in USD 20-50 + USD 50-100 + USD 100-200 combined), roughly mirroring where legit volume also concentrates — no extreme low/high-value skew. Fraud transactions average slightly higher (USD 149.24 vs USD 134.51, +11%), but the distributions overlap heavily — TransactionAmt alone is a weak standalone discriminator. Useful in combination with other features (as later confirmed by SHAP), not as a rule on its own.

3.2.1 Key Numerical Variables — TransactionDT (Temporal)¶

Second half of 3.2: is fraud rate stable over time, or does it drift/spike across the ~180-day window covered by the dataset?

In [10]:
# 3.2 Key Numerical Variables — TransactionDT (Temporal)

# Convert TransactionDT to days
df_train['day'] = df_train['TransactionDT'] // (24*60*60)

daily_fraud_rate = df_train.groupby('day')['isFraud'].mean()

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 4))
plt.plot(daily_fraud_rate.index, daily_fraud_rate.values,
         color=COLORS['fraud'])
plt.title('Daily Fraud Rate Over Time')
plt.xlabel('Day')
plt.ylabel('Fraud Rate')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Fraud rate isn't flat — it swings roughly 0.01-0.07 day to day, with a visible dip around day ~25-30 and a cluster of spikes around day ~110-120. No clear long-term trend (not steadily rising/falling), just noisy fluctuation around a ~3.5% baseline. Worth remembering for modeling: day-level info alone is noisy, but the derived calendar features (hour, day_of_week, month, is_weekend — built in 5.3) may capture more stable sub-patterns than raw daily rate does.

3.3 Categorical Variables — Systematic EDA (tiered by cardinality)¶

37 categorical vars detected programmatically (dtype + known numeric-encoded ones: card1-6, addr1-2, M1-9) — no manual selection. Split into 3 tiers by cardinality (≤10 / 10-100 / >100 categories), each plotted/reported the way that actually fits its scale: full bar charts, top-15+Other, or reliability-filtered summary tables for the identifier-like ones (card1, DeviceInfo, etc.).

In [11]:
# 3.3 Categorical Variables — Systematic EDA (tiered by cardinality)

# Detect categorical variables
dtype_categorical = df_train.select_dtypes(include=['object', 'category']).columns.tolist()

known_numeric_categorical = [
    'card1', 'card2', 'card3', 'card5',   # card4/card6 already object dtype
    'addr1', 'addr2',
] + [c for c in df_train.columns if c.startswith('M')]  # M1-M9 flags

categorical_vars = sorted(set(dtype_categorical + known_numeric_categorical)
                           & set(df_train.columns))
categorical_vars = [c for c in categorical_vars if c != 'isFraud']

print(f"Detected {len(categorical_vars)} categorical variables:")
print(categorical_vars)

# Cardinality profile
cardinality = df_train[categorical_vars].nunique().sort_values(ascending=False)
print("\nCardinality (unique values per variable):")
print(cardinality.to_string())

LOW_MAX    = 10    # plot every category
MEDIUM_MAX = 100   # plot top-15 + "Other"
# > MEDIUM_MAX: identifier-like, summary table instead of a chart

tier_low    = cardinality[cardinality <= LOW_MAX].index.tolist()
tier_medium = cardinality[(cardinality > LOW_MAX) & (cardinality <= MEDIUM_MAX)].index.tolist()
tier_high   = cardinality[cardinality > MEDIUM_MAX].index.tolist()

print(f"\nTier LOW    (≤{LOW_MAX} categories, plot all):        {len(tier_low)} vars")
print(f"Tier MEDIUM ({LOW_MAX}-{MEDIUM_MAX}, top15 + Other):  {len(tier_medium)} vars → {tier_medium}")
print(f"Tier HIGH   (>{MEDIUM_MAX}, summary table only):      {len(tier_high)} vars → {tier_high}")

BASELINE = df_train['isFraud'].mean()

# Fraud rate table with reliability filtering
def fraud_rate_table(df, var, top_n=None, min_n=None):
    """Fraud rate + sample size per category.
    - top_n: keep only the N most frequent categories, bucket rest into 'Other'
    - min_n: additionally fold any category with fewer than min_n rows into 'Other',
             even if it would otherwise make the top_n cut (avoids noisy small-sample bars)
    """
    counts = df[var].value_counts(dropna=False)

    keep = counts.index
    if top_n is not None and len(counts) > top_n:
        keep = counts.head(top_n).index
    if min_n is not None:
        keep = counts[counts >= min_n].index.intersection(keep)

    bucketed = df[var].where(df[var].isin(keep), other='Other')
    grp = df.assign(_cat=bucketed).groupby('_cat', observed=True)['isFraud']
    return grp.agg(fraud_rate='mean', n='count').sort_values('n', ascending=False)


def plot_tier(varlist, top_n, title, n_cols=3, figsize_row=5, min_n=None):
    n_vars = len(varlist)
    if n_vars == 0:
        return
    n_rows = int(np.ceil(n_vars / n_cols))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(7.5 * n_cols, figsize_row * n_rows))
    axes = np.array(axes).reshape(-1) if n_vars > 1 else np.array([axes])

    for ax, var in zip(axes, varlist):
        table = fraud_rate_table(df_train, var, top_n=top_n, min_n=min_n)
        ax.bar(range(len(table)), table['fraud_rate'],
               color=COLORS['fraud'], alpha=0.85, edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.6)
        ax.axhline(y=BASELINE, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.2)
        ax.set_xticks(range(len(table)))
        ax.set_xticklabels(table.index.astype(str), rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=12)
        ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=11)
        ax.set_ylabel('Fraud rate', fontsize=13)
        ax.set_title(f'{var} (n_categories: {cardinality[var]})', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
        for i, (rate, n) in enumerate(zip(table['fraud_rate'], table['n'])):
            ax.text(i, rate, f'{n:,}', ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')

    for ax in axes[n_vars:]:
        ax.set_visible(False)

    plt.suptitle(title, fontweight='bold', fontsize=20, y=1.0)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# Tier LOW: split into thematic groups for readability
m_flags   = [v for v in tier_low if v.startswith('M')]
id_flags  = [v for v in tier_low if v.startswith('id_')]
other_low = [v for v in tier_low if v not in m_flags + id_flags]

plot_tier(m_flags, top_n=None,
          title='Fraud Rate by Category — Low Cardinality: M-Flags (Match Indicators)',
          n_cols=3, figsize_row=5)

plot_tier(id_flags, top_n=None,
          title='Fraud Rate by Category — Low Cardinality: Identity Binary Flags (id_)',
          n_cols=3, figsize_row=5)

plot_tier(other_low, top_n=None,
          title='Fraud Rate by Category — Low Cardinality: Other Variables',
          n_cols=3, figsize_row=5)

# Tier MEDIUM: top 15 + Other, folding low-sample categories too
MIN_N_MEDIUM = 200

plot_tier(tier_medium, top_n=15, min_n=MIN_N_MEDIUM,
          title=f'Fraud Rate by Category — Medium Cardinality ({LOW_MAX}-{MEDIUM_MAX} categories, min n={MIN_N_MEDIUM})',
          n_cols=2, figsize_row=5)

# Tier HIGH: identifier-like variables — reliability-filtered summary
MIN_N_HIGH = 500
TOP_K      = 8

print("=" * 70)
print("Fraud Rate by Category — High Cardinality (identifier-like variables)")
print(f"Bar charts are not used here: these variables have too many unique")
print(f"values for direct visual inspection. Only categories with n≥{MIN_N_HIGH}")
print(f"are reported, to avoid presenting small-sample noise as signal.")
print("=" * 70)
print()

high_card_summary = []

for var in tier_high:
    table = fraud_rate_table(df_train, var, top_n=None)
    reliable = table[table['n'] >= MIN_N_HIGH].copy()

    n_total          = len(table)
    n_reliable       = len(reliable)
    pct_rows_covered = reliable['n'].sum() / len(df_train) * 100

    high_card_summary.append({
        'variable':          var,
        'n_categories':      cardinality[var],
        'n_reliable_cats':   n_reliable,
        'pct_rows_covered':  round(pct_rows_covered, 1),
        'max_fraud_rate':    round(reliable['fraud_rate'].max(), 4) if n_reliable else None,
        'min_fraud_rate':    round(reliable['fraud_rate'].min(), 4) if n_reliable else None,
    })

    print(f"--- {var} (n_categories: {cardinality[var]}, "
          f"{n_reliable}/{n_total} categories have n≥{MIN_N_HIGH}, "
          f"covering {pct_rows_covered:.1f}% of rows) ---")

    if n_reliable == 0:
        print("  No category meets the minimum sample size — skipping.\n")
        continue

    print(f"  Highest fraud rate (top {TOP_K}):")
    print(reliable.sort_values('fraud_rate', ascending=False)
          .head(TOP_K)[['fraud_rate', 'n']].to_string())
    print(f"\n  Lowest fraud rate (bottom {TOP_K}):")
    print(reliable.sort_values('fraud_rate', ascending=True)
          .head(TOP_K)[['fraud_rate', 'n']].to_string())
    print()

# Overview table across all high-cardinality variables
summary_df = pd.DataFrame(high_card_summary)
print("Tier HIGH — reliability overview:\n")
summary_df

5 id_31 130 31 22.3000 0.2184 0.0015
6 card5 119 22 98.4000 0.1472 0.0082
7 card3 114 8 98.9000 0.1307 0.0153

3.3 Categorical Variables — Key Findings

Low cardinality:

  • M-flags: M4="M2" and M5="T" show the clearest deviation from baseline (~0.11 and ~0.036 fraud rate). M1's "F" category (n=25) and other tiny bins should be read with caution — sample too small to trust.
  • id_ flags: consistent pattern — "Found"/"T" categories tend to have higher fraud rates than "New"/"NotFound"/"F" across id_15, id_16, id_28, id_29, id_35, id_37. id_23 (proxy type) stands out: "Anonymous" ~0.14 vs ~0.05-0.06 for Transparent/Hidden, though all three have modest sample sizes (<3.5k). id_27 "NotFound" (n=14) and id_34 "match_status_-1" (n=3) are noise, not signal.
  • ProductCD: "C" is the clear outlier (0.12 vs baseline 0.035), "W" the safest (0.02) and by far the most common (440k rows).
  • card6: "credit" (0.070) roughly 3x riskier than "debit" (0.023); the other two categories have n<30, ignore.
  • card4: "discover" stands out (0.075) but on a small base (n=6,651) — worth a caveat.
  • DeviceType: mobile (0.10) noticeably riskier than desktop (0.065).

Medium cardinality — biggest single finding of 3.3:

  • R_emaildomain = outlook.com hits 0.165 fraud rate (n=2,507) — ~4.7x baseline, the strongest categorical signal found so far. icloud.com also elevated (0.13).
  • P_emaildomain = outlook.com echoes this at a lower level (0.10, n=5,096).
  • addr2 = 96.0 (0.14) and 60.0 (0.09) stand out against the dominant 87.0 (0.024, 98% of rows) — but both minority categories have low volume relative to the base.
  • id_30 (OS): "Other" and less common OS versions (Windows 8.1, iOS 11.3.0) skew high; mainstream OS (Windows 10, Windows 7) sit near or below baseline.

High cardinality (identifier-like, table-based, min n=500):

  • card1 (199 reliable, 59.5% coverage): widest spread — 0.0 to 0.333. Strong candidate for frequency/target encoding.
  • card2 (107 reliable, 87.2% coverage): even wider spread (0.0009–0.3606), with good coverage. Likely one of the most useful high-cardinality predictors once encoded.
  • addr1 (54 reliable, 88.2% coverage): moderate spread (0.008–0.084), well covered.
  • card5 (22 reliable, 98.4% coverage): near-full coverage, meaningful spread (0.008–0.147).
  • card3 (8 reliable, 98.9% coverage): coverage high only because two categories (150, 185) cover ~98% of rows — effectively near-binary despite 114 nominal categories.
  • DeviceInfo (7 reliable, only 15.4% coverage): too fragmented as-is — needs regrouping (e.g. OS family) before it's usable.
  • id_33 / screen resolution (20 reliable, 11.4% coverage): same fragmentation issue — mobile/uncommon resolutions skew high (1280x720: 0.137), common desktop resolutions skew low (2560x1440: 0.008).
  • id_31 / browser (31 reliable, 22.3% coverage): Firefox highest (0.218), IE11-tablet lowest (0.0015) — real signal, but raw strings too granular; grouping by browser family/platform likely more useful than raw category.

Takeaway: card1/card2/addr1/card5 are well-covered and worth encoding directly. DeviceInfo/id_33/id_31 carry real signal but are too sparse in raw form — feature engineering (grouping, frequency encoding) needed before they're usable.

3.4 Missingness Map by Group (C, D, M, V, and Other/Named)¶

Shifting from values (Sections 3.1-3.3) to missingness itself.

Scope: C, D, M, V cover the anonymized/semi-anonymized IEEE-CIS blocks, which share generic letter+number naming. D excludes DeviceType/DeviceInfo (bug caught earlier — those two start with "D" but are device/categorical fields, not time-deltas). Named variables (card, addr, id_, email domains, TransactionAmt/DT, etc.) are added here as a fifth "Other" group purely for completeness of this missingness map — most of them were already examined individually in Sections 3.2-3.3, and id_ missingness specifically is explored in depth in Section 3.5.

Coverage is checked programmatically (377 + 56 = 433 / 433 columns), so nothing is silently left out. The heatmap below is drawn on a 5,000-row sample, since the full matrix is too wide to render meaningfully; the numeric summary that follows is computed on the full dataset.

3.4 Missingness Map — Key Findings

  • C-features: 0% missing across all 14 — fully populated block, confirmed by the solid purple heatmap.
  • D-features: highly heterogeneous (0.2%–93.4%, avg 58.2%) — some D columns nearly complete, others almost entirely absent. This is the block explored in depth via _present flags in 3.5.
  • M-features: more uniform than D (28.7%–59.4%, avg 49.9%) — all M columns carry a comparable, moderate missing rate.
  • V-features: widest block (339 cols), avg 43.0%, full range 0%–86.1% — consistent with the NaN-similarity grouping approach used in 3.6.
  • Other (named vars): highest average missingness of all groups (65.2%!), driven mainly by the id_* block (most transactions have no identity data at all — consistent with has_identity flag created in feature engineering).
  • Visual pattern across D/V/Other: missingness shows clear vertical banding — entire transactions (columns in the heatmap) tend to be missing many features at once, not random scattered dropout. This points to structural missingness (e.g. identity data only collected for a subset of sessions) rather than per-field data quality issues — reinforces why missingness itself is treated as signal in 3.5.

3.5 Missingness as a signal¶

3.4 showed how much is missing per group — now: does missingness itself predict fraud? Compare fraud rate when a field is missing vs. present, per column (D/M/Other) or per NaN-pattern group (V, reusing groups from feature engineering logic). Filtered on both effect size (>2%) AND statistical significance (chi-square, p<0.01) AND sample size (n≥200 both sides).

In [13]:
# 3.5 Missingness as a signal 
import re
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency

# Reuse the exact same group definitions as 3.4 
d_cols_no_device = [col for col in df_train.columns
                     if col.startswith('D') and col not in ('DeviceType', 'DeviceInfo')]

feature_groups_34 = {
    'C': [col for col in df_train.columns if col.startswith('C')],
    'D': d_cols_no_device,
    'M': [col for col in df_train.columns if col.startswith('M')],
    'V': [col for col in df_train.columns if col.startswith('V')],
}
all_cols_34 = set(df_train.columns) - {'isFraud', 'TransactionID'}
covered_34  = set().union(*feature_groups_34.values())
feature_groups_34['Other'] = sorted(all_cols_34 - covered_34)

BASELINE = df_train['isFraud'].mean()
MIN_N = 200

def group_label(col, feature_groups):
    for grp, cols in feature_groups.items():
        if col in cols:
            return grp
    return 'Unknown'

def natural_key(col):
    """Sort within family by numeric suffix (D1, D2,...D15 — not D1, D10, D11...)."""
    m = re.match(r'^([A-Za-z_]+?)(\d+)$', col)
    if m:
        prefix, num = m.groups()
        return (prefix, int(num))
    return (col, 9999)


# Column-by-column analysis (D+M, Other)

def compute_missingness_signal(cols, feature_groups, min_n=MIN_N):
    results = []
    for col in cols:
        is_null = df_train[col].isnull()
        n_null, n_not_null = is_null.sum(), (~is_null).sum()
        if n_null == 0 or n_not_null == 0:
            continue

        fraud_null     = df_train.loc[is_null, 'isFraud'].mean()
        fraud_not_null = df_train.loc[~is_null, 'isFraud'].mean()
        signed_diff    = fraud_null - fraud_not_null

        contingency = pd.crosstab(is_null, df_train['isFraud'])
        if contingency.shape == (2, 2):
            _, p_value, _, _ = chi2_contingency(contingency)
        else:
            p_value = np.nan

        reliable = (n_null >= min_n) and (n_not_null >= min_n)

        results.append({
            'column':         col,
            'group':          group_label(col, feature_groups),
            'fraud_null':     round(fraud_null, 4),
            'fraud_not_null': round(fraud_not_null, 4),
            'signed_diff':    round(signed_diff, 4),
            'abs_diff':       round(abs(signed_diff), 4),
            'n_null':         n_null,
            'n_not_null':     n_not_null,
            'pct_missing':    round(is_null.mean(), 4),
            'p_value':        round(p_value, 6) if pd.notna(p_value) else np.nan,
            'significant':    bool(p_value < 0.01) if pd.notna(p_value) else False,
            'reliable_n':     reliable,
        })
    df_res = pd.DataFrame(results)
    if not df_res.empty:
        df_res['sort_key'] = df_res['column'].map(natural_key)
        df_res = df_res.sort_values('sort_key').drop(columns='sort_key')
    return df_res


def plot_missingness_signal_chunked(df_subset, title, chunk_size=30,
                                     bar_width_in=0.32, row_height=5):
    if df_subset.empty:
        print(f"No columns with missing values in group: {title}")
        return
    n_total  = len(df_subset)
    n_chunks = int(np.ceil(n_total / chunk_size))
    fig_width = max(14, bar_width_in * chunk_size * 2)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_chunks, 1, figsize=(fig_width, row_height * n_chunks))
    axes = np.atleast_1d(axes)

    for i in range(n_chunks):
        chunk = df_subset.iloc[i * chunk_size : (i + 1) * chunk_size]
        ax = axes[i]
        x = range(len(chunk))
        ax.bar([j - 0.2 for j in x], chunk['fraud_null'],
               width=0.4, label='Missing', color=COLORS['neutral'], alpha=0.8)
        ax.bar([j + 0.2 for j in x], chunk['fraud_not_null'],
               width=0.4, label='Not missing', color=COLORS['fraud'], alpha=0.8)
        ax.axhline(y=BASELINE, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.2)
        ax.set_xticks(list(x))
        labels = [f"{c}*" if not r else c
                  for c, r in zip(chunk['column'], chunk['reliable_n'])]
        ax.set_xticklabels(labels, rotation=90, ha='center', fontsize=9)
        ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=10)
        ax.set_ylabel('Fraud rate', fontsize=11)
        if i == 0:
            ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc='upper right')

    plt.suptitle(f'{title}  (* = sample size below reliability threshold, n<{MIN_N})',
                 fontsize=16, fontweight='bold', y=1.0)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


dm_cols    = feature_groups_34['D'] + feature_groups_34['M']
other_cols = feature_groups_34['Other']

results_dm    = compute_missingness_signal(dm_cols, feature_groups_34)
results_other = compute_missingness_signal(other_cols, feature_groups_34)

# ── Plot: D & M columns
plot_missingness_signal_chunked(
    results_dm, 'Fraud Rate: Missing vs Non-Missing — D & M columns', chunk_size=30)

# ── Plot: Other (named) columns
plot_missingness_signal_chunked(
    results_other, 'Fraud Rate: Missing vs Non-Missing — Other (Named) Variables', chunk_size=30)


# Part 2 — V columns, grouped by NaN-similarity pattern
def compute_nan_similarity_groups(cols, df):
    """Groups columns sharing an identical missingness pattern (same rows
    missing/present). Returns a dict: group_label -> list of columns."""
    null_mask = df[cols].isnull()
    patterns = null_mask.T.apply(lambda row: row.values.tobytes(), axis=1)
    pattern_groups = {}
    for col, pattern in patterns.items():
        pattern_groups.setdefault(pattern, []).append(col)

    labeled = {}
    for cols_in_group in pattern_groups.values():
        cols_sorted = sorted(cols_in_group, key=natural_key)
        label = cols_sorted[0] if len(cols_sorted) == 1 else f"{cols_sorted[0]}-{cols_sorted[-1]}"
        labeled[label] = cols_sorted
    return labeled


def compute_missingness_signal_grouped(nan_groups, df, min_n=MIN_N):
    results = []
    for label, cols_in_group in nan_groups.items():
        rep_col = cols_in_group[0]
        is_null = df[rep_col].isnull()
        n_null, n_not_null = is_null.sum(), (~is_null).sum()
        if n_null == 0 or n_not_null == 0:
            continue

        fraud_null     = df.loc[is_null, 'isFraud'].mean()
        fraud_not_null = df.loc[~is_null, 'isFraud'].mean()
        signed_diff    = fraud_null - fraud_not_null

        contingency = pd.crosstab(is_null, df['isFraud'])
        if contingency.shape == (2, 2):
            _, p_value, _, _ = chi2_contingency(contingency)
        else:
            p_value = np.nan

        reliable = (n_null >= min_n) and (n_not_null >= min_n)

        results.append({
            'group_label':    label,
            'n_columns':      len(cols_in_group),
            'fraud_null':     round(fraud_null, 4),
            'fraud_not_null': round(fraud_not_null, 4),
            'signed_diff':    round(signed_diff, 4),
            'abs_diff':       round(abs(signed_diff), 4),
            'n_null':         n_null,
            'n_not_null':     n_not_null,
            'pct_missing':    round(is_null.mean(), 4),
            'p_value':        round(p_value, 6) if pd.notna(p_value) else np.nan,
            'significant':    bool(p_value < 0.01) if pd.notna(p_value) else False,
            'reliable_n':     reliable,
        })
    df_res = pd.DataFrame(results)
    if not df_res.empty:
        df_res['_order'] = df_res['group_label'].apply(lambda l: natural_key(l.split('-')[0]))
        df_res = df_res.sort_values('_order').drop(columns='_order')
    return df_res


def plot_missingness_signal_bygroup(df_subset, title):
    if df_subset.empty:
        print(f"No groups to plot for: {title}")
        return
    n = len(df_subset)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(max(14, 0.5 * n), 6))
    x = range(n)
    ax.bar([i - 0.2 for i in x], df_subset['fraud_null'],
           width=0.4, label='Missing', color=COLORS['neutral'], alpha=0.8)
    ax.bar([i + 0.2 for i in x], df_subset['fraud_not_null'],
           width=0.4, label='Not missing', color=COLORS['fraud'], alpha=0.8)
    ax.axhline(y=BASELINE, color='black', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.2, label='Baseline (3.5%)')
    ax.set_xticks(list(x))
    labels = [f"{l} (n={n_cols}){'*' if not rel else ''}"
              for l, n_cols, rel in zip(df_subset['group_label'],
                                          df_subset['n_columns'],
                                          df_subset['reliable_n'])]
    ax.set_xticklabels(labels, rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=10)
    ax.tick_params(axis='y', labelsize=11)
    ax.set_ylabel('Fraud rate', fontsize=13)
    ax.set_title(f'{title}  (* = sample below reliability threshold, n<{MIN_N})',
                 fontsize=15, fontweight='bold')
    ax.legend(fontsize=10)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


v_nan_groups = compute_nan_similarity_groups(feature_groups_34['V'], df_train)
print(f"V columns ({len(feature_groups_34['V'])}) collapse into {len(v_nan_groups)} "

for label, cols in v_nan_groups.items():
    print(f"  {label:20s}  ({len(cols)} columns)")

results_v_grouped = compute_missingness_signal_grouped(v_nan_groups, df_train)

# Plot: V columns (grouped)

    results_v_grouped, 'Fraud Rate: Missing vs Non-Missing — V columns (grouped by NaN pattern)')

3.5 Missingness as Signal — Key Findings

  • D-features: the strongest reliable missingness signal in the whole dataset. D7 shows the largest gap of any single column (missing: 0.027, not-missing: 0.149 — more than 5x). D6, D8, D9, D12, D13, D14 all show a consistent pattern: when populated, fraud rate roughly quadruples vs. baseline. This directly validates the _present flags built in Section 5.1.
  • M-flags: opposite direction — missingness itself (not presence) correlates with higher fraud for M1, M2, M3, M6, M8, M9 (roughly 2-3x baseline when missing). Consistent with the _missing flags in 5.1.
  • addr1/addr2: identical numbers for both — likely because they share the exact same missingness pattern (same rows null in both). Fraud rate roughly 5x higher when missing (0.118 vs 0.025).
  • id_ block (Other + V): dominant pattern across virtually the entire id_* block — missing means LOWER fraud rate (+-0.02-0.03), present means HIGHER (+-0.08). This is the strongest, most consistent signal in the section: presence of identity/device data is itself predictive, validating has_identity from 5.1.
  • V column groups: 339 columns collapse cleanly into 15 NaN-similarity groups. V169-V210, V167-V216, V217-V278, V220-V272 all echo the id_ pattern (missing → lower fraud). V1-V11 and V53-V74 go the other way (missing → higher fraud).
  • Verified — V279-V321 excluded correctly: visually the largest gap (missing 0.1667 vs. not-missing 0.0350), but n_null=12 (only 2 fraud cases) → p=0.090, fails both the reliability and significance filters. Textbook case of effect size without evidence — correctly dropped from the "significant" table.

3.6 V columns — correlation structure and NaN similarity groups¶

Building on the missingness patterns identified across the V-column NaN-similarity groups in Section 3.5, this section computes and visualizes a correlation matrix for each group in order to identify highly correlated columns (candidates for dropping) preserving the informational content already characterized above, including the missingness signal captured separately via the flags built in Section 5.1.

In [17]:
# 3.6 V columns — correlation structure within NaN similarity groups
# Reuses v_nan_groups computed in Section 3.5

v_corr_groups = list(v_nan_groups.values())
v_cols = [c for g in v_corr_groups for c in g]

print(f"Number of NaN similarity groups: {len(v_corr_groups)}")
print(f"\nGroup sizes:")
for i, g in enumerate(sorted(v_corr_groups, key=len, reverse=True)):
    pct = df_train[g[0]].isnull().mean()
    print(f"  Group {i+1:2d}: {len(g):3d} columns — {pct:.1%} missing — {g[:5]}{'...' if len(g)>5 else ''}")

# Correlation heatmap per group
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 5, figsize=(20, 12))
axes = axes.flatten()
redundancy_summary = []
for i, group in enumerate(sorted(v_corr_groups, key=len, reverse=True)):
    ax = axes[i]

    # Sample for speed if group is large
    sample = df_train[group].dropna()
    if len(sample) > 50000:
        sample = sample.sample(50000, random_state=SEED)

    corr = sample.corr().abs()

    # Count highly correlated pairs (>0.9)
    upper = corr.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape), k=1).astype(bool))
    high_corr_pairs = (upper > 0.9).sum().sum()

    # How many columns we could drop (keep 1 per highly correlated pair)
    # Note: within each correlated pair, the retained column is simply the
    # first one encountered in corr.columns order, not selected by any
    # information-content criterion.

    to_drop = set()
    for col in corr.columns:
        if col in to_drop:
            continue
        correlated = upper[col][upper[col] > 0.9].index.tolist()
        to_drop.update(correlated)

    redundancy_summary.append({
        'group':           i + 1,
        'n_cols':          len(group),
        'pct_missing':     round(df_train[group[0]].isnull().mean(), 3),
        'high_corr_pairs': int(high_corr_pairs),
        'can_drop':        len(to_drop),
        'keep':            len(group) - len(to_drop),
    })

    # Heatmap
    sns.heatmap(corr, ax=ax, cmap='Blues', vmin=0, vmax=1,
                xticklabels=False, yticklabels=False,
                cbar=False, square=True)
    ax.set_title(f'G{i+1}: {len(group)} cols, {df_train[group[0]].isnull().mean():.0%} null',
                 fontsize=8)
plt.suptitle('V Columns — Correlation Structure by NaN Similarity Group',
             fontweight='bold', fontsize=12)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Summary table

print(summary_df.to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nTotal V columns:       {len(v_cols)}")
print(f"Total can drop:        {summary_df['can_drop'].sum()}")
print(f"Total to keep:         {summary_df['keep'].sum()}")
print(f"Dimensionality reduction: {summary_df['can_drop'].sum()/len(v_cols):.1%}")

3.6 V Columns — Correlation Structure — Key Findings

  • 339 V columns collapse into 15 NaN-similarity groups (same grouping as 3.5) — internal correlation checked within each group (threshold >0.9).
  • Drop criterion is correlation only. Missingness % is shown alongside each group for descriptive context, but plays no role in the actual drop decision — a column is only removed for being highly correlated (>0.9) with another column already kept in its group.
  • Groups 10, 11, 14 (86.1% missing each): also the most redundant (11-15 droppable columns each) — but this is a coincidence, not causation. High missingness and high redundancy happen to co-occur here, they are not linked by the method.
  • Group 3 proves the point: 0% missing, yet still the 2nd-highest redundancy in the block (62 high-corr pairs, 17/32 droppable). Fully populated groups can be just as redundant as sparse ones — this is about Vesta's engineered features overlapping, not about missing data.
  • Groups 1, 4, 8, 12 (~76-78% missing): echo the id_-like missingness signal found significant in 3.5 (V169-V210, V167-V216, V217-V278, V220-V272). Dropping redundant columns here doesn't lose that signal — it's captured separately via the _present/has_identity flags in 5.1.
  • Total: 150/339 columns dropped (44.2%), confirmed identical in 5.4 (feature engineering) — dataset shrinks from 434 to 304 columns after V reduction.
  • Notice: which column survives within a correlated pair is order-dependent (greedy selection by column order, not by information content) — noted as a methodological limitation, not treated as optimal.

3.7 Numerical Variables (C, D) — Distribution and Outliers¶

In this section, we examine the distributions of the C and D features themselves — outliers (IQR-based) and correlation with isFraud — complementing the missingness-focused analysis of 3.4-3.6. This section reuses the same C/D definitions established in Section 3.4 for consistency.

In [18]:
#  3.7 Numerical Variables (C, D) — Distribution and Outliers
c_cols = [col for col in df_train.columns if col.startswith('C')]
d_cols = [col for col in df_train.columns
          if col.startswith('D') and col not in ('DeviceType', 'DeviceInfo')]

BASELINE = df_train['isFraud'].mean()

# Summary statistics table
def numeric_summary(cols, df):
    rows = []
    for col in cols:
        series = df[col].dropna()
        if series.empty:
            continue
        q1, q3 = series.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
        iqr = q3 - q1
        lower_bound = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
        upper_bound = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
        n_outliers = ((series < lower_bound) | (series > upper_bound)).sum()

        rows.append({
            'column':        col,
            'mean':          round(series.mean(), 2),
            'median':        round(series.median(), 2),
            'std':           round(series.std(), 2),
            'min':           round(series.min(), 2),
            'max':           round(series.max(), 2),
            'skew':          round(series.skew(), 2),
            'n_outliers_iqr': int(n_outliers),
            'pct_outliers_iqr': round(n_outliers / len(series) * 100, 2),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values('column', key=lambda s: s.map(natural_key))

summary_c = numeric_summary(c_cols, df_train)
summary_d = numeric_summary(d_cols, df_train)

print("C-features — descriptive summary:")
print(summary_c.to_string(index=False))
print("\nD-features — descriptive summary:")
print(summary_d.to_string(index=False))

# Boxplots — distribution & outliers, fraud vs legit
def plot_boxplots_by_class(cols, title, n_cols=5, figsize_row=4):
    n_vars = len(cols)
    n_rows = int(np.ceil(n_vars / n_cols))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(n_rows, n_cols, figsize=(4 * n_cols, figsize_row * n_rows))
    axes = np.array(axes).reshape(-1) if n_vars > 1 else np.array([axes])

    for ax, col in zip(axes, sorted(cols, key=natural_key)):
        data_to_plot = [
            df_train.loc[df_train['isFraud'] == 0, col].dropna(),
            df_train.loc[df_train['isFraud'] == 1, col].dropna(),
        ]
        bp = ax.boxplot(data_to_plot, labels=['Legit', 'Fraud'],
                         patch_artist=True, showfliers=True, widths=0.6)
        for patch, color in zip(bp['boxes'], [COLORS['legit'], COLORS['fraud']]):
            patch.set_facecolor(color)
            patch.set_alpha(0.7)
        ax.set_title(col, fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
        ax.tick_params(axis='both', labelsize=10)

    for ax in axes[n_vars:]:
        ax.set_visible(False)

    plt.suptitle(title, fontweight='bold', fontsize=16, y=1.0)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

3.7 Numerical Variables (C, D) — Key Findings

  • C-features: extreme right skew across the board (skew 5.6–88.9), 7-24% "outliers" by IQR — but these are likely legitimate count-type values (transaction/device counts), not data errors. Despite this, essentially NO linear correlation with fraud (all |r| < 0.04). Pearson correlation is a poor fit for such skewed distributions — tree-based models (used in Section 6) are better suited to exploit any non-linear signal here.
  • D-features: real, consistent correlation with fraud — all negative, D8 (-0.143) and D7 (-0.127) strongest. Higher D-value → lower fraud probability, once the value is present.
  • Interesting nuance vs. Section 3.5: presence of D7/D8 correlates with HIGHER fraud (found in 3.5), but among transactions where they ARE present, a HIGHER value correlates with LOWER fraud. Not a contradiction — two separate signals: whether the field exists (risk factor) vs. what it's worth once it does (protective factor, larger time-deltas ~ more established activity).
  • D2, D9, D11: 0 outliers by IQR — consistent with their low skew (near 1.0 or below), not an error.
